title: The Aeneid
author: Virgil
openingChapterLabel: Book I — Arms and the Man
openingText: I sing of arms and the man, he who, exiled by fate, first came from the coast of Troy to Italy, and to Lavinian shores — hurled about endlessly by land and sea, as the gods willed, battered by the anger of cruel Juno, suffering much in war, until he founded a city and brought his gods to Latium.
about: Troy has fallen. Aeneas is told by the gods that he must sail to Italy and found a new city. He doesn't want to — he has a queen who loves him, a past he cannot release, and a destiny he did not choose. The Aeneid is about what it costs a man to become the instrument of history.

angleCards.title: The price of destiny.
angleCards.text: Aeneas is called "pious" more than any other character — but his pietas requires him to leave Dido, abandon the past, and subordinate everything personal to a future he will not live to see. The poem keeps the cost visible.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what it costs Aeneas to fulfil his destiny — what he sacrifices, who he abandons, and whether the poem endorses or mourns those costs.

angleCards.title: Dido's tragedy.
angleCards.text: She is the most fully realised character in the poem — a brilliant queen who loves the wrong man at the wrong moment. Her books (I and IV) are the emotional heart of the Aeneid. What Aeneas does to her is not presented as simple.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this through Dido — what Rome's founding requires of the women in Aeneas's path, and whether the poem knows it is condemning her.

angleCards.title: Homer's shadow.
angleCards.text: Books I–VI echo the Odyssey; Books VII–XII echo the Iliad. Virgil knew his readers would hold both in their heads. Notice where Aeneas is a lesser hero than Odysseus or Achilles — and ask whether that is a flaw or the whole point.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Aeneid as a response to Homer — what Virgil borrowed, what he changed, and what a Roman epic values differently from a Greek one.

angleCards.title: Duty as a philosophy of life.
angleCards.text: Pietas is what makes Aeneas Roman rather than Greek. The poem invites you to ask whether a man who suppresses all personal desire for collective purpose is admirable or hollow — and never quite gives you a clean answer.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine pietas — duty to gods, family, and state — as the Aeneid's central value, and whether it is presented as heroic or oppressive.

cast.name: Aeneas
cast.description: Trojan prince, survivor, reluctant founder of Rome. He does what fate and gods require. Whether this makes him heroic or hollow is the question the poem never cleanly resolves.

cast.name: Dido
cast.description: Founder of a great city, brilliant ruler, and the woman Aeneas loves and must leave. Her tragedy is not incidental to the poem — it is its emotional centre.

cast.name: Turnus
cast.description: The Italian warrior who stands between Aeneas and his destiny. He is not simply a villain — he has legitimate grievances and genuine heroism. The poem's final act belongs to him.

cast.name: Juno
cast.description: Queen of the gods, implacable enemy of Troy and everything Aeneas represents. She drives the plot through sheer divine stubbornness for twelve books — and never quite loses.

cast.name: Venus
cast.description: Aeneas's divine mother and counterweight to Juno. She protects him without being able to remove his suffering — the gods in the Aeneid are powerful but not omnipotent over fate.

cast.name: Anchises
cast.description: Aeneas's mortal father, who dies before Italy is reached. His appearance in the underworld in Book VI — showing Aeneas the future of Rome — is the philosophical heart of the poem.
